one_liner: Rust ribbon-filter crate: about 7.6 bits/key at 0.8% FPR, less than Bloom, with cache-local 'pleated' construction.
what_it_does: A Rust crate of static approximate-membership filters (ribbon filters). You build one once from a slice of u64 keys and then call contains(u64): there are no false negatives, and false positives occur at about 2^-R. It has two families, homogeneous Ribbon<R> (w=64, construction never fails) and StdRibbon<R> (w=128, the RocksDB shape, with a seed-retry loop and a Result return). Each has arrival, pleated and parallel constructors that produce bit-identical filters, plus contains_batch, Hash-trait wrappers (from_hashable/contains_hashable) and a checksummed to_bytes/from_bytes format. It is not a drop-in Bloom replacement, because nothing can be inserted after the build.
how_it_is_fast: The memory win comes from the ribbon filter itself (Dillinger and Walzer; banded GF(2) linear system solved by on-the-fly Gaussian elimination). Homogeneous w=64 ribbon costs about 1.09*R bits/key. The companion preprint puts Bloom at about 44% over the minimum, which works out to roughly 10 bits/key at R=7 against 7.6 here. The speed contribution is 'pleating' (partition-instead-of-sort): one counting-sort pass buckets keys by start slot into 2^16-slot windows (about 768 KiB) before banding. That turns the dependent, cache-missing row-reduction chains of arrival-order banding into cache-local work, and because the banding solution is order-independent the output is bit-identical. from_keys_parallel splits the slot range across std threads and defers keys within 2^14 slots of a range boundary (plus any spills) to a sequential tail, following parallel BuRR.
when_to_use: Static key sets rebuilt in bulk (immutable LSM/SST files, periodic snapshots, deduplication indexes) where filter RAM or disk size matters more than build CPU.
Filters of about 10M+ 64-bit keys, where the banding table outgrows L3 and pleating pays off: 26.0 vs 60.4 ns/key at 10M in the crate's own benchmark.

When you want the false-positive rate tunable in 1-bit steps (R from 1 to 32), e.g. R=7 at about 7.6 bits/key and 0.8% FPR, or R=10 at about 10.9 bits/key and 0.1%, rather than fixed 8/16-bit fingerprints.
Rust services that persist filters and want a versioned, checksummed blob whose decoder rejects corrupt or mismatched input with typed errors (fuzzed and Miri-checked in CI).
Multi-core build machines that want a parallel build they can check: from_keys_parallel output is bit-identical to the sequential build.
when_not_to_use: The key set changes or its final size is unknown. The filter is build-once, with no insert, delete, union or counting; use a Bloom, cuckoo or quotient filter.

Build time must match Bloom. In the companion preprint's C++ harness, pleated ribbon is still about 24 ns/key at 100M keys against 6.1-11.5 ns/key for single-thread blocked-Bloom insertion, and it takes 16 threads (11.9 ns/key) to catch up. In this crate, 8 threads give only 24.4 vs 26.0 ns/key over single-thread pleated at 10M.
Small filters, where the banding table fits in cache. At 1M keys pleated is slower than arrival order (26.1 vs 23.8 ns/key), and from_hashable always uses the pleated path.

Lookup latency is the bottleneck. No Bloom query comparison is measured, and each probe reads up to 2*R u64 words (112 bytes at R=7) against one cache line for a blocked Bloom filter. The crate reports 17.4 ns scalar and 15.4 ns batched miss-dominated lookups at 10M keys (standard w=128: 24.2 ns).

You need proven production maturity. It has 1 GitHub star, 21 crates.io downloads, 0 reverse dependencies and a single author, has had no commits since 2026-07-12, and its companion paper is an unreviewed preprint.

integration.dependencies: xxhash-rust 0.8 (xxh3 feature) only; requires std (not no_std). The default feature 'parallel' uses std::thread with no extra crates.
integration.platforms: Pure Rust, any target. CI runs tests on Linux, macOS and Windows plus i686-unknown-linux-musl (32-bit). The software prefetch in contains_batch is only compiled on x86_64; other architectures run batch queries without prefetch.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The source shows filters are immutable Vec-backed structs with no interior mutability, so concurrent contains() through shared references should be safe (inferred, not stated). from_keys_parallel takes an explicit thread count and uses scoped std threads.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it answers the same 'possibly present' question with no false negatives, but it needs the full key set up front, supports no insert or delete after the build, keys the API on u64 (or process-local Hash), and uses its own PLT1 serialization format

gotchas: The from_hashable/contains_hashable path hashes Rust Hash output with fixed-seed xxh3. The crate warns this is only reliable within the same process, target and toolchain, so do not persist such filters. For durable filters, hash a stable encoding to u64 yourself.
The hash seed is fixed and non-cryptographic. SECURITY.md says an adversary who chooses the queried keys can inflate the false-positive rate, so keyed hashing is your job.

Peak build memory is well above the final filter (derived from the source). A pleated w=64 build copies the whole key slice (8 B/key) and allocates about 1.09n u64 coefficient rows (about 8.7 B/key). StdRibbon allocates a u128 coefficient row plus a u32 result row per slot, re-bands every key on each seed retry (up to 64 seeds), and returns BuildError::NoSolvingSeed if none solves.
Filter sizing is fixed by n and R at build time, and bits_per_key(n) needs you to pass n back in. An empty key set still produces a non-empty filter.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick pleat over xorf (about 9 bits/key at 0.4% for BinaryFuse8) when you are in Rust and want a static filter with a tunable R and slightly less space (about 8.75 bits/key at R=8, derived from the crate's sizing formula), and your large rebuilds can use the pleated or parallel build. Choose BuRR or RocksDB Ribbon (C++) when you need sub-1% space overhead or a battle-tested production implementation, and fastbloom or Boost.Bloom when keys arrive incrementally or lookup and build speed matter more than bits/key.
verified_claims_summary: The crate's own Criterion benchmarks on an Intel i9-14900HX (rustc version and flags not stated) measure a homogeneous w=64, R=7 filter at about 7.6 bits/key with a measured 0.783% FPR. They also show pleated construction at 26.0 ns/key vs 60.4 for the crate's own arrival-order build at 10M 64-bit keys (2.3x), and slightly slower at 1M (26.1 vs 23.8). No Bloom filter is measured in the crate. The 'less memory than Bloom' claim is analytical, and the companion preprint's C++ measurements show pleated ribbon construction still slower than single-thread blocked-Bloom insertion.
status_note: A new single-author research release: repository created 2026-07-11, last main-branch commit 2026-07-12 with Dependabot PRs left open since, v0.1.0 on crates.io. It is dual MIT/Apache-2.0, tested byte-for-byte against the fastfilter_cpp reference kernel, fuzzed, Miri-checked and under a 90% coverage gate, so it is usable as a dependency or small enough (about 2.4k lines of Rust source, tests included) to vendor, but it has no track record of production use.
